items.description_text: The project aims to strengthen the quality of digital youth work by helping youth workers respond confidently to AI-shaped realities in young people’s lives, while using digital tools to widen - not limit - meaningful youth participation. In youth work practice, this means youth workers are better able to facilitate sessions where young people can critically engage with misinformation/deepfakes and online influence, participate safely in digital spaces, and express their voice through creative and participatory methods. Through this project, our overall aim is to strengthen the quality of digital youth work by equipping youth workers to support young people’s participation in AI-shaped online environments in a safe, ethical and inclusive way. Therefore, we'll address the following objectives: O1. Build youth workers’ practical competences in digital youth work and AI literacy (deepfakes/misinformation, online influence, responsible use of tools) so they can address these topics with young people confidently. O2. Improve youth workers’ facilitation skills to run participatory, non-formal sessions that strengthen youth voice online and offline (co-creation, dialogue, critical thinking, meaningful participation). O3. Strengthen organisational practice by introducing simple, usable routines for privacy and consent, safeguarding in digital/hybrid settings, and inclusion-by-design (including low-tech alternatives). O4. Produce and test ready-to-run youth work session formats and practical checklists that can be replicated by colleagues and adapted across partner contexts. O5. Ensure transfer to daily work through one follow-up pilot activity implemented by each partner organisation, supported by peer exchange and light coordination after the mobility (internal sharing with colleagues encouraged). items.title: PLAY IS HUMAN RIGHT – The neuroscience of joy and the NVC practice of connection
items.summary: Inspired by Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience and Nonviolent Communication (NVC), this webinar explores how the PLAY system supports connection, resilience, creativity, and emotional wellbeing.
items.participants_countries: Erasmus+ Youth Programme countries , Other countries in the world , Partner Countries Neighbouring the EU
items.fee_text: no
items.description_text: In Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience, PLAY is one of the brain’s primary emotional systems—a neural circuit that supports connection, flexibility, learning, resilience, and social trust. And yet, in many adult lives, especially in work, parenting, leadership, and intimate relationships, play often disappears first. During this webinar, we will explore the PLAY circuit through the lens of Nonviolent Communication (NVC). Together, we will discover why play requires a sense of safety, how joy differs from entertainment or performance, and how a playful presence can soften tension, open space for dialogue, and support our needs for connection, freedom, creativity, ease, and belonging. We will also ask: What happens to our relationships when play is absent? Why do we sometimes lose access to lightness, curiosity, and spontaneity? How can sharing NVC help us bring play back without forcing it, bypassing pain, or pretending everything is okay? Where playfulness can support sharing and learning NVC? This webinar is for people who want to understand play not as a luxury, but as a deep human need and a powerful doorway to empathy, regulation, and more alive relationships. It is a result of the Erasmus + training course “Flying Giraffes” that took place in Poland in June 2026. You can register here: https://www.fundacjamudita.org/en/play-is-human-right-the-neuroscience-of-joy-and-the-nvc-practice-of-connection-with-paulina-orbitowska-fernandez/

items.description_text: Do you sometimes feel overwhelmed by your emotions and wish you could understand them better? Would you like to respond to difficult situations with more awareness, empathy, and choice? Emotions are not something to fix, hide, or “manage away.” They are signals that tell us what matters, what hurts, what we long for, and what may need our attention. In this webinar, we will explore emotions through the lens of Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We will look at how to recognise and name feelings, listen to the needs beneath them, stay present when emotions become intense, and move from automatic reaction towards greater connection and conscious choice. IN THIS WEBINAR, YOU WILL EXPLORE: how to understand and embrace emotions with empathy; how NVC can help us recognise feelings and underlying needs; simple ways to regulate yourself in difficult moments; how to respond with more awareness and choice. The session will combine accessible theoretical input with reflection and practical tools that you can bring into everyday life and your work with others.

items.description_text: Play for Human Rights is an international training course for youth workers taking place in Dobczyce, Poland, from 23 to 31 October 2026. The project will bring together 24 youth workers from eight countries for a seven-day learning programme focused on Human Rights Education (HRE), Intercultural Learning (ICL) and democratic participation. The central methodology of the training will be an immersive, long-form role-play simulation. Through experiential learning, participants will explore human dignity, equality, discrimination, cultural diversity, democracy and civic engagement. They will learn how to design, facilitate and debrief educational simulations that foster empathy, critical thinking, intercultural dialogue and active citizenship among young people. The programme will combine practical exercises, role-play, group reflection, structured debriefing, self-assessment and collaborative design. Participants will strengthen their competences in facilitation, programme development, intercultural communication, inclusion, evaluation and safe and ethical youth-work practice, in line with the European Training Strategy Competence Model for Youth Workers. Throughout the training, participants will co-create and test at least five transferable workshops addressing human rights, discrimination, equality, diversity and democratic participation. The developed methods will be suitable for adaptation to different youth-work settings and to the needs of young people with fewer opportunities, including young people from migrant, Roma, rural and NEET backgrounds. The project will also support participating organisations in integrating simulation-based Human Rights Education and Intercultural Learning into their regular activities. After the training, participants will be expected to transfer the acquired knowledge to their local communities, organise follow-up activities and contribute to the dissemination and visibility of the project and its results. items.description_text: Context Human rights educators, activists, and youth workers across Europe navigate an increasingly unpredictable context. Shrinking civil society spaces, systemic uncertainty, and financial instability create high-stress environments that directly impact psychological well-being. This ongoing strain often leads to professional burnout, affecting both individual educators and the long-term sustainability of youth organisations and their work. This 7-day training course offers a dedicated space for youth workers to step back, address work-related stress, build emotional resilience, and discover actionable tools to safeguard their mental well-being—and the well-being of the young people they support. We are bringing together youth workers, trainers, and activists to step off the treadmill, address the psychological weight of our work, and build practical emotional resilience. It is not about standard self-care; it’s about discovering collective, realistic tools to protect our well-being and keep our organisations sustainable while learning how to better support the young people we work with. items.description_text: Creative Circles: Voices is an exploratory training course for youth workers, educators, mentors, facilitators and trainers working in the field of non-formal learning and youth work. The training explores voice as a tool for self-expression, connection and participation. Through music, singing, rhythm, improvisation, storytelling and embodied practices, participants will explore their relationship with their own voice, what they want to express, what may be difficult to express, and what happens when different voices meet. The learning journey moves from the individual towards the collective through three main focuses: Finding My Voice, Expressing My Voice and Voices Together. Participants will work with body, breath, resonance, movement, sound and silence, as well as collective singing, storytelling and improvisation. We will also explore questions of participation: who gets heard, who remains silent, and how youth workers can create spaces where young people feel able to find and use their own voices. The training is based on experiential and non-formal learning. Participants will learn by doing, experimenting, reflecting and creating together rather than learning how to sing or perform. A significant part of the programme will take place outdoors, using nature as an active element of the learning process. Throughout the week, visiting practitioners will introduce different approaches to voice, music and storytelling. Together, participants will also collect and document methods and exercises that can be adapted and used in their own youth work practice. No previous musical, singing or storytelling experience is required. The training is intended for people actively involved in youth work and non-formal learning who are curious about using creative and embodied approaches in their work with young people.

Youth engagement is increasingly recognised as a decisive force in achieving Europe’s green transition. Both formal (school systems, civic participation structures) and informal (community projects, youth work) pathways empower young people to contribute to environmental action. The European Green Deal support initiatives emphasise that youth bring creativity, fresh perspectives, and a direct stake in long‑term climate solutions, making their involvement indispensable. items.description_text: What does it take to be both seen and safe in Europe's nightlife, music and cultural scenes? Across Greece, Cyprus, Bulgaria and Ireland, we reached out to the artists and community members who make these scenes come to life, diving deep into their experiences of belonging and community, identity and visibility, harassment and safety. This 90-minute online workshop shares what we found, but not in the way you'd expect. Rather than going through slides and statistics, we’ll step into the research itself through playful improv and an open conversation with the researcher behind our study. Safety remains one of the biggest challenges in urban entertainment and it's something we have to keep building together, especially for women and LGBTI+ people. items.description_text: What if sport could do more than move people? What if it could move society forward? Sport for Sustainable Development is an international Training Course bringing together youth workers, sport coaches, educators and facilitators who want to explore the potential of sport beyond physical activity. During the training, participants will discover Education Through Sport (ETS) through practice and theory and explore how sport and non-formal education can be used to address the Sustainable Development Goals, social responsibility and active citizenship. But this is not a training where you simply sit, listen and take notes. The learning process is built around experiential learning, movement, reflection, peer learning and co-creation. Participants will experience educational sport activities themselves, analyse the learning behind them and gradually build a practical toolbox of methods that can be transferred to their own organisations and communities. Working in international teams, participants will then take the next step: designing their own Education Through Sport activities connected to sustainable development, testing and improving them together, and finally facilitating them with young people at a local school. In this way, ideas developed during the training will be transformed into real educational practice. Along the way, participants will strengthen their facilitation, teamwork, communication, activity-design, reflection and leadership competences, exchange practices from different countries and build an international professional network. Grow personally and professionally. And return home ready to give something back to your organisation, your community and the young people you work with. If you believe that sport can be more than competition and want to learn how to turn movement into meaningful learning and positive change – this training course is for you! :)

items.description_text: The Training Course will explore the role of youth work in supporting the career development and empowerment of young people living in rural and smaller communities in a rapidly changing world. For many rural young people, career choices are shaped not only by fewer local opportunities, but also by deeply rooted perceptions about what is possible: “there is nothing for me here,” “to succeed I have to leave,” “entrepreneurship is for people with money or connections,” or “a good career means finding a secure job.” At the same time, digitalisation, AI, remote work and new forms of entrepreneurship are changing what it means to build a career and where opportunities can be created. YOUTH WORK CREATE will focus on the role youth work can play in challenging these limiting narratives and building a different mindset. The course approaches entrepreneurial spirit not simply as starting a business, but as a way of thinking and acting — being curious, taking initiative, recognising opportunities, solving problems, experimenting, learning from failure and having the confidence to turn ideas into action. It will also explore social entrepreneurship, encouraging young people to see challenges in their communities not only as reasons to leave, but also as opportunities to create solutions, services and positive local change. Participants will explore and test non-formal education techniques, methods and approaches for working with young people's mindsets: identifying and challenging stereotypes and limiting beliefs, discovering strengths and local resources, developing creativity and initiative, building resilience, exploring different career and entrepreneurial pathways, and moving from ideas towards action. items.description_text: A waiting room. A youth centre. A public square. A restroom. A courtroom. Most spaces used by young people are designed by adults. Adults decide what is needed, what feels safe and what feels welcoming. But how often do we ask young people what they think? And more importantly, how often do we invite them to create these spaces with us? The idea for this training comes from a cocreation project in which four unaccompanied minors worked with judges, guardians and children's rights experts to redesign a courtroom for the Belgian Council for Alien Law Litigation. Their ideas helped create a space that felt calmer, clearer and more respectful. The project showed that when young people are treated as equal partners, everyone benefits, including the adults who use and work in these spaces. Why does this matter? The spaces young people use every day influence how they feel, act and connect with others. When they help shape these spaces, they build confidence, ownership and a stronger sense of belonging. At the same time, the whole community can benefit from spaces that better reflect the needs and experiences of the people who use them. This training explores how youth workers can set up cocreation processes that enable young people to actively shape the spaces around them. Moving beyond participation, we focus on working together, sharing responsibility and creating solutions that reflect young people's experiences and needs. Many STEAM activities start with a predefined outcome: build a bridge, create a vehicle, follow these instructions. Storybuilders Lab explores a different approach. The facilitator defines the learning intention, but participants influence the story, identify the problem and decide what needs to be created. The methodology follows a simple learning cycle: STORY → QUESTION → IDEAS → CHALLENGE → DESIGN → MAKE → TEST → IMPROVE → REFLECT → STORY CONTINUES Participants will learn how to use story triggers, mystery objects and open questions to generate curiosity and meaningful challenges. They will explore Story Democracy, a participatory method for collecting, combining and developing different ideas so that the direction of a project is not predetermined by the facilitator or dominated by the strongest voices in the group. A central part of the course is hands-on prototyping. Participants will work with accessible materials such as cardboard, recyclable materials and simple construction tools to turn ideas into physical prototypes. Makedo or similar cardboard-construction tools may be used where available, but no specialised equipment is required. The focus is not on creating a perfect final object. Participants practise an iterative process of: Make → Test → Notice → Change → Test again This allows them to explore how experimentation, “failure”, debugging and redesign can become valuable learning experiences in youth work. items.description_text: Call for participants for this years Global Education Lab: Skill share 03. – 10. November 2026 in Bern, Switzerland. This November, we are bringing people together from all over the world to share methods, knowledge and strategies for combating the global «care crisis» – and to develop educational formats together. Global Education Lab is an annual series of skillshare weeks for educators working on global justice, neocolonialism and global supply chains. The skillshare focuses on critical and decolonial pedagogy. It has been organised by Service Civil International since several years. About the Training Our focus this year is care and indigeneity. In a world driven by extraction and profit, the «Care Crisis» has become a global phenomenon: essential work like parenting, healthcare, and community maintenance is undervalued. This directly relates to the lack of care we give to our planet. Meanwhile, Indigenous Peoples, who safeguard 80% of the world’s remaining biodiversity, continue to face dispossession, criminalization, and the erasure of their knowledge systems. Throughout the week, participants will: Exchange knowledge on Indigenous resistance and land defence. Explore examples of environmental and Indigenous human rights defenders. Discuss alternative economic models based on the commons, reciprocity and Sumak Kawsay (Good Living). Co-create educational methods and workshop materials that connect global justice, care and Indigenous perspectives for youth education. The Lab aims to strengthen the international Global Education network while developing practical educational resources that participants can adapt and use in their own communities. Practicalities Who can participate? Educators, youth workers or activists working on global justice, neocolonialism or global supply chains. items.description_text: This course explores how youth work can become genuinely inclusive — moving beyond a declarative discourse on diversity towards everyday practice. Starting from the participants' own experience, we examine the common pitfalls that organisations, programmes and facilitators fall into (tokenism, surface-level or performative inclusion, assuming a space is neutral, one-size-fits-all approaches, accessibility treated as an afterthought, unconscious bias in recruitment and facilitation) and we build concrete solutions for designing learning and growth environments that value diversity. The methodology is non-formal and experiential, based on reflection, case studies and transfer to each participant's own context. Across Europe, youth workers increasingly encounter young people experiencing stress, anxiety, loneliness, burnout, and other mental health challenges. While youth workers are often a trusted source of support, many feel they lack practical tools and confidence to respond effectively. MindBoost Academy has been designed to strengthen their competences through experiential learning, international cooperation, and the exchange of good practices. A central outcome of the training is the co-creation of the MindBoost Toolkit—a practical collection of methods, activities, facilitation guides, and resources that participants will design together throughout the week. Rather than simply testing existing materials, participants will actively contribute their own experiences, ideas, and expertise to develop tools that can be adapted and implemented in youth work settings across different communities. During six days in Breda, participants will: - strengthen their understanding of youth mental health and wellbeing; - explore practical, non-formal education methods for promoting resilience and emotional wellbeing; - develop facilitation, mentoring, and peer-support skills; - learn how to recognise challenges and respond appropriately within the role of a youth worker; - co-create the MindBoost Toolkit, ensuring it reflects diverse experiences and practical needs from both partner countries; - build lasting connections with fellow youth workers and organisations. items.description_text: NGO Awero team, Nexes Interculturals, Cities of Learning Network partners, and the International Youth Work Trainers Guild are offering a 6th modular training for trainers, aligned to the European Training Strategy (ETS) competence model. The training course will contribute to the development of the ETS trainers’ competences in the area of “Being Civically Engaged”. Understanding and asserting the trainer's work as an act of civic engagement Connecting relevant [youth] policies and educational programmes to own values, beliefs and different political perspectives Reflecting on personal civic engagement, values and beliefs, and integrating them in the training practice in a responsible and constructive way Supporting learners in developing critical thinking and using the diversity of opinions and beliefs as a source of learning Applying democracy and human rights principles in the design and delivery of training activities. Programme of the training course The programme opens with introductions, setting the learning stage, and exploring participants' personal values and beliefs, then links these to trainer identity and active citizenship. Midweek, the group will travel to Barcelona to explore civic engagement and local training practices, including a Migrantour optional session in one of Barcelona’s neighbourhoods. The later days shift to developing pilot civically engaged training practice ideas, examining diversity, democracy and human rights as sources of learning, and covering resources for trainers' professional development and recognition. Please check the draft programme attached to this call for participants. items.description_text: Humour is already present in youth work practice - but it's rarely used as a deliberate, structured tool. "Humour is Serious Business" (HiSB) is a 6-day Erasmus+ KA153-YOU training course (27 November - 3 December 2026, Hollókő, Hungary) that will help you turn something you probably already do instinctively into an intentional, ethical, and effective competence for engaging young people. This training is aimed specifically at practitioners in the field of non-formal learning and youth work - not at the general public. You should apply if you are a youth worker (professional or voluntary), a youth leader, a young person (18+) with leadership potential already identified by your organisation, or a practitioner with relevant expertise who works with young people (e.g. a coach, mentor or tutor), even if youth work is not your primary profession. Through non-formal methods - World Café, simulations and role play, clowning and improvisation, team building, and daily reflection groups - you will explore the many different types of humour, examine cultural differences in how humour is used, reflect on your own sense of humour, and develop concrete post-programme actions to bring back to your own community. Every participant leaves with a Personal Development Plan and the chance to earn a Youthpass. HiSB is delivered by an experienced international Training Team and hosted by MAVISZ (Hungary), together with partner organisations in Poland, Portugal, Armenia, Serbia, Latvia, Croatia, Montenegro and Spain. 36 participants will take part, 4 per sending country. Full details, including the daily programme, participant support structure, and reimbursement process, are in the Info Pack: https://mavisz.my.canva.site/hisb2026

items.description_text: Why this programme? Young people increasingly experience the world through digital, visual, interactive and participatory media. At the same time, heritage education can sometimes remain centred on traditional formats: guided tours, exhibitions, historical information and passive observation. This creates an opportunity for youth work. New media can provide alternative entry points into heritage, allowing young people to: explore places and stories through immersive experiences; discover hidden or forgotten narratives; connect personal and community memories with wider European heritage; question dominant interpretations of history; create their own narratives; collaborate across cultures; transform physical spaces into interactive learning environments. The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. Specific objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Explore contemporary approaches to cultural heritage and heritage awareness. Identify opportunities for using immersive and interactive media in youth work. Experiment with VR, AR, 360° media, projection mapping, interactive installations, digital storytelling and other creative technologies. Design non-formal education activities connecting young people with local, national and European heritage. Use storytelling and participatory methodologies to make heritage more relevant to young people. Encourage young people to question, reinterpret and remix heritage narratives. items.description_text: How can international youth mobility become truly safe, inclusive, and empowering for Highly Vulnerable Young People? A course for youth workers, facilitators, and organisations to learn how to create safer, more inclusive, and trauma-informed international mobility experiences for Highly Vulnerable Young People (HVYP). This is a self-paced and practice-oriented online course for professionals working in youth mobility and non-formal education. The course supports participants in developing the competencies needed to responsibly include and support young people facing multiple and intersecting barriers in international programmes. You are going to learn about: safer and more inclusive mobility environments, safeguarding and risk management in practice, trauma-informed and solution-focused approaches, recognising and preventing harm and exclusion, supporting HVYP before, during, and after mobility experiences, professional boundaries, crisis response, and self-care in youth work. About this course International youth mobility projects can create powerful opportunities for learning, participation, connection, and personal growth. At the same time, for highly vulnerable young people, unfamiliar international environments may also involve increased vulnerability and risk. This course was developed within the LADDER project to support youth workers and organisations in creating mobility experiences that are not only accessible, but genuinely safe, supportive, and empowering. Through practical examples, case studies, reflection exercises, and field-tested approaches, participants will strengthen their capacity to: create safer and more inclusive mobility projects, anticipate and prevent risks, respond responsibly to challenging situations, and support young people facing multiple barriers. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition. The event will take place outdoors and is aimed at educators, activity leaders, and facilitators. In Brittany, 27 participants are expected.
